Fury Warrior has received several major changes in WoW Forever, both directly and indirectly. The most important of these is the changes made to Rage Generation; Rage in WoW Forever is now normalised, similar to the changes made in Cataclysm originally. This means that attacks generate a static amount of rage within a set range based on a formula; rage is no longer tied to direct auto-attack damage dealt, and critical strikes do not generate additional rage. As such, our rage generation does not scale with gear, and the only way to increase the amount of rage gained is to take additional damage. This will result in our rage generation being severely lower when compared to other versions of Classic Fury Warrior, which reduces the number of skills and abilities we can use. We must now be far more careful with our rage usage, and cannot use abilities as frequently as before.

In addition, enemies' armor cannot be reduced as much as before, as|s9907|and|s11717|no longer stack with their armor reduction effects. This substantially lowers our damage even further, especially as we are tied entirely to physical damage and do not possess any baseline magical damage-dealing spells or abilities.

flow.v: On initial glimpse, Fury Warrior may seem relatively similar to its counterpart in baseline Classic - it maintains the same rotation, plays roughly the same talent build, and features very few changes or additions to its kit. However, when you take a closer look, Fury Warrior appears to be in a very rough spot at end-game content upon deeper analysis.

The removal of world buffs is a large blow to Fury Warrior, which was one of the strongest scaling specs in the game. In addition, Rage normalization heavily restricts our packed ability usage, and the increased armor on bosses reduces our damage further. Group Composition is now more important than ever - crucial group buffs like|s10614|and|s17007|are even more important than ever to perform, as their relative power has been massively increased due to the lack of other stats.

Our abilities have also received some notable changes -|s23881|has been nerfed, despite its already weakened state due to the lower attack power we can gain. Improved Battle Shout has also been removed as a talent, which reduces our group utility. Perhaps most notably, our signature DPS Cooldown,|s1719|has received zero changes to its cooldown, remaining at 30 minutes, while comparable cooldowns such as|s417141|have a three-minute cooldown.

In areas where it is strong, namely low target cleave, Warrior excels and is undoubtedly without equal. However, it will suffer in prolonged single-target fights, especially when there is little to no incoming damage.

Previously, Retribution Paladin was a rather weak class with little class identity and modest support offerings to raid and party members. Forever seeks to address these issues with the introduction of a revitalized talent tree, new spells & abilities, and has reworked existing ones to make them much more powerful and substantial.

Of the new abilities and talents, the most interesting and impactful are surelyHoly Strike- our new instant attack which deals Holy damage - andTwist of Light, our current Retribution talent tree capstone that allows you to benefit from two seals on a single auto-attack by weaving back and forth between them.

cells: A new instant attack that deals Holy damage based on weapon damage and spell power; similar to Crusader Strike. A new mainstay primary ability for damage-dealing.

flow.v: One goal for Forever is to make every class and specialization viable. While we currently do not have that much information on what sort of viability Retribution will have at max level, we can make some educated guesses. Similar to many other branches of WoW Classic, it appears at first glance that Retribution will have moderate damage-dealing capabilities while offering strong support and utility benefits to raid and party members for PvE content, as well as the ability to easily tank or heal as an off-spec or in an emergency.

For PvP content, it seems likely that Retribution will continue to be a front-loaded damage-dealer with moderate mobility and strong support & utility buffs, but a lack of major damage-dealing cooldowns.

The main role of the Retribution Paladin is a damage-dealer that can do moderate DPS while supporting the raid with blessings, auras, and utility spells - and our strengths & weaknesses are going to reflect that primary role. Our main role is not to top the damage meters, unfortunately, as we lack a major damage cooldown that would enable it.

flow.v: While high-level Retribution gameplay will have a moderately complex rotation compared to other classes, it will still be rather easy for new players to learn and adjust to, especially at lower levels. The class design is currently very straightforward and has only a limited learning curve, allowing new Paladins to easily pick up the class even if they have never played it before. Forever, in general, seems to be rather friendly and accessible to new players.

Paladin is also a class that is strongest when supporting other players, and grants new players the ability to provide lots of benefits to their friends and teammates, which they will be very happy to have, such as dispels or blessings.
The main class system for Retribution Paladin in Forever is the capstone talent:|s1310735|. Therefore, I will take a short section to explain how it works. Fear not, it is rather simple.

This|s1310735|mechanic is a much easier version of "seal twisting" from other branches of WoW Classic, and allows you to benefit from multiple seals on a single auto-attack. Since seals are abilities that add damage to your melee attacks, this capstone talent allows you to switch into a new seal while still gaining the effects of the previous seal via this "Echo" mechanic, and on your next melee attack, it will benefit from both the new seal you cast as well as the "Echo" of your previous seal - effectively allowing you to have two seals on a single attack.

This is going to be the core mechanic behind Retribution gameplay at higher levels, as it is currently understood. Compared to other versions of "seal twisting", it is much simpler, though it no longer has a swing-timing or rhythm-based element, and therefore player opinions have been mixed regarding it. Luckily, Blizzard has added a swing timer to the base UI in order to facilitate this playstyle properly. We hope to get underway testing this talent as soon as possible and will report back with more information.

flow.v: Hunters are easy to pick up for any player, and out of the three specs in Forever, Survival won't be any different, although the spec will only start to shine around level 32 due to the talent requirements. You will probably always have a button to press, with only the occasional choice of which one to press first to be made. You will most likely be able to choose to play with or without a pet as Survival Hunter. A fun part of Hunter is the high ceiling they have, especially in solo content and PvP. If you become proficient enough at using your full kit of Ranged and Melee abilities, you can be very annoying to deal with. Good control of traps and stings will make you strong in PvP. And lastly, good pet and environment control makes you very powerful in solo content and allows you to solo things other classes can not. This is true for all three Hunter specs.

Forever keeps that kit and adds tools that cover split damage and reward swapping heals, while removing a few of the old talent and race gates. Healing Focus, Improved Prayer of Healing, and Lightwell are gone from the Holy tree. Binding Heal, Prayer of Mending, and Litany of Light take their place. cells: Binding Heal is a new Holy talent. It heals a friendly target and the caster at the same time, with low threat, on a 1.5-second cast.

One of the most ambitious stated goals of the World of Warcraft: Forever development team was to provide new tools to elevate traditionally underpowered specializations. With the changes coming in Forever, it is clear that Shadow Priest is receiving some major changes as a direct result of this philosophy. In Classic, despite its popularity as a solo-PvP or "dueling" spec, Shadow Priest has a reputation as one of the weakest damage dealers in end-game raiding, typically brought only as a one-off to buff Warlock damage.

While much of the game still has yet to be discovered, it is apparent that the development team has added a variety of changes directly aimed at improving Shadow Priest's viability as a damage dealer in endgame PvE, while ultimately maintaining Shadow's core identity.
World of Warcraft: Forever introduces a number of new and interesting abilities to the Priest class that were not originally available in the Classic game.

cells: Shadow Word: Death is an iconic Shadow Priest ability first introduced in The Burning Crusade, which has been added to Forever as a baseline Priest spell obtainable at level 32. Shadow Word: Death provides the perfect tool to finish off low-health enemies as you aim to trigger|s15270|, and with two points invested in|s1310076|, Shadow Word: Death becomes a strong execute-style rotational ability on a short 15-second cooldown.

Dark Sacrifice is one of several new Priest Racial abilities added in Forever, which provides the Undead Priest with an effect similar to the Warlock's|s1454|ability, converting Health to Mana over 15 seconds. While it's unclear exactly how powerful this ability will feel in practice, especially given its lengthy 10-minute cooldown, this ability is undoubtedly a natural fit for the Shadow Priest toolkit.

Contingency Plan is another new Priest Racial ability granting the Gnome Priest a targetable defensive buff which shields and heals over time when a target drops to low Health. Assuming Contingency Plan can be used in Shadowform, this ability is a particularly interesting external defensive option that can be used in a pinch either on an ally or yourself.

flow.v: Shadow Priests in WoW: Forever will enjoy a number of reworked and updated abilities and talents designed to improve overall viability and quality-of-life as a damage dealing specialization.

cells: Devouring Plague is now a baseline spell for Priest on a shorter one-minute cooldown. Previously, Devouring Plague was a three-minute cooldown available only to Undead Priests.

Shadowform has essentially been completely reworked: Shadowform increases Shadow damage by only 10% (down from 15%), but now also reduces the Mana cost of Shadow spells by 50%, and increases the critical strike damage bonus of Shadow spells by 100%. Additionally, only healing spells cannot be cast in Shadowform, allowing you to cast Holy damaging and utility spells without dropping Shadowform. The 15% reduction to incoming Physical damage remains unchanged.

Vampiric Embrace is now on a one-minute cooldown and lasts for 30 seconds, but has an added effect of activating Spirit Tap when an affected enemy dies. This provides Shadow Priests with a more consistent way to activate Spirit Tap in group play, especially during Raid encounters with adds where it is highly impractical to achieve last-hits on enemies.

Shadow Weaving has been reworked and no longer increases all Shadow spell damage taken by the target. Instead, it simply now increases the caster's Shadow damage dealt. This is a substantial change from the Classic version, as this talent historically encouraged raid groups to bring exactly one Shadow Priest to provide this effect regardless of their overall damage output. This shifts the dynamic in endgame PvE back towards a focus on the Shadow Priest's individual damage output, which has been a major theme across the game's new approach to class design.

flow.v: While it's clear that the Forever development team has made changes to Shadow Priest aimed directly at improving its endgame PvE viability, it remains to be seen exactly how that will shake out in practice.
Here are some of the most apparent strengths and weaknesses of Shadow Priest based on what is currently available:

cells: Strong solo PvP presence- Shadow Priest has a toolkit particularly well-suited for one-on-one PvP and this is unlikely to change in Forever.Brand new Mana recovery tools- Shadow Priest has traditionally been highly Mana intensive, but many of the changes to Shadow in Forever are aimed at addressing the spec's Mana economy.Bring on the Execute damage- The addition of Shadow Word: Death and supporting talent Early Demise provide Shadow with a new damage niche aimed at quickly dispatching enemies below 20% Health.

Arcane Mage is overall a pretty satisfying specialization, it's biggest negative is leveling. Players typically level up as frost or fire and then swap to arcane in other expansions where all three are relevant. Your overall performance is also very tightly dependent on your guild and raid dps; this can be a positive for some players who enjoy performing to their best within the limiting factors they find themselves in, while for other players it can feel infuriating because they could be performing a lot better in fights with shorter kill times where mana management is easier or not relevant at all.

cells: Burst Potential- With cooldowns such as Arcane Power and the talents buffing Arcane Critical Damage, in endgame, there's a very high chance that Arcane will have great Burst damage (which has historically been true).Fluid Rotation- Although more of a feel thing, using Arcane Blast to stack up its debuff followed by a quick Arcane missiles feels very satisfying and is a great gameplay loop.Mana Management- Many people enjoy this aspect of Arcane, having skill expression being shown by your ability to use mana effectively to maximize damage/uptime.

Mana issues- Although it can be a positive, for people who struggle with mana management, going OOM can feel extremely infuriating.Bad Leveling- Because the spells can be very expensive mana-wise, you'll often find yourself using Wand instead - which still has good damage, but you could do that as any specialization.Fight Length Depending- Having your performance tied so much to the specific bosses and/or your guild's overall performance - limiting your kill time can be very frustrating.

flow.v: Akin to the other Mage specializations in Classic WoW, this "new" specialization in Forever feels very simple initially; whether or not it gets more complicated, it's hard to know - it could be as simple as Arcane Blasting to 4 stacks and using buffed Arcane Missiles to clear the stacks, or it could require some sort of spell in between to remove stacks when you have bad luck with getting the proc. It could also very well require adapting your rotation depending on boss kill time, by changing the total amount of Arcane Blast stacks you're willing to use each time to maximize your mana usage for higher overall uptime of your most relevant spells.
My guess is on the former, and it remains very simple, given the game seems extremely simple within the spirit of vanilla WoW so far, but hard to be certain.
While leveling, wanding feels very relevant while leveling, but that's always been the case for every caster. Arcane having a wand specialization talent just boosts that further early on.

While doing dungeons, the AoE feels amazing and is by far the highlight of the specialization, with high threat reduction from|s11210|, allowing you to use Arcane Explosion as much as you want without having much consideration for threat, assuming you're playing with a good tank (ideally a paladin tank). It did require some adaptation to make sure I was consistently good on mana in dungeons; this was done by using wand or low-cost spells, such as only using one Arcane Blast followed by Arcane Missiles right away, or just using wand to save mana for pulls where mana was more effectively used on AoE.

Personally, this specialization feels pretty good for new players, since it's initially very simple, and further optimization is mostly just to avoid taking breaks to drink, which most groups will be more than fine doing. If it does become more difficult later, it won't be by much, I believe, and you'll have plenty of time to get used to it while leveling to max level later on.

At the very early levels, you can simply wand enemies to death and then use Wake of Fire Fireblast at the start of combat of the following enemy, repeating the cycle of:

It did require some adaptation to make sure I was consistently good on mana in dungeons; this was done by using wand often after pre-casting pyro and using the Wake of Fire proc from a previous mob dying, to save mana for pulls where mana was more effectively used on AoE with Flamestrike followed by Arcane Explosion.

v.text: - is one of the main mechanics within Fire Mage specialization. Whenever you critical strike with a non-periodic spell, it turns 40% of that damage into a damage-over-time effect. This essentially transforms the talent into something entirely passive, not requiring any gameplay changes at all. Essentially making the specialization a lot simpler for the majority of the player base.

Additionally, it reduces the cast time of Pyroblast by 25% per stack up to 3 stacks. This is changed from past versions of the talent where it made it instant. Stacking up said procs with your main spell and then using a fast-cast Pyroblast will be a key part of the rotation.

- is your personal debuff to put onto enemies; this stacks up to 15% damage done by fire spells and will be a key part of maximizing your damage. Make sure to keep the debuff active without letting it drop during Boss Fights.

flow.v: In WoW: Forever, one of the stated design goals is to make every spec viable in any content, so far Frost feels perfectly fine up to level 20. As things progress, I'll update this post, but all 3 Mage specs feel mostly on-par with one another, and none seem left behind when it comes to the wider 9 classes either.

Frost has a strong niche as the master of the ranged slow and an all-around tanky caster that is just as effective in AOE as single target. There are some weaknesses that we have overall in that we cannot sustain ourselves well and lack the burst of Arcane and Fire. Lastly, a larger weakness that comes up fairly often in classic is that the mob immunity or resistance state may have us favoring Frostfire Bolt when it's available in some cases, or just not playing Frost as a primary for certain encounters.

cells: Tough to Kill- Frost Mages are the quintessential safety caster in WoW; Frost spells slow enemies, making them much easier to kite and DPS with no personal risk. Ice Barrier and Ice Block add an additional layer of defensive power that isn't ignorable.Group Utility- Unlike other Mages, Frost Mages will have easy access to Cold Snap, doubling the impact of things like Frost Nova and Ice Block in an instant can make or break situations.Mobility- Compared to the classic rotation, the inclusion of Ice Lance will open up a lot of instant GCDs that can be used to optimize movement.AOE- Mages are kings when it comes to AOE; Frost Mage fits that motif well, bringing heavy slows with its bread-and-butter AOE spell.

Self-Healing- Frost Mages tend to suffer a bit against rot damage historically in WoW; Forever isn't looking to change that, and we still lack a proper health recovery skill in combat.Burst- Frost Mages within our own tree lack a proper cooldown like Arcane Power or Combustion.Immune Enemies- Frost Mages rely heavily on enemies being able to take Frost damage without having raised resistances or immunities. When enemies do have a Frost immunity, much of our talent spend goes to waste while we use other school spells.

There are two sensible approaches one can consider: you can take two gathering professions and buy what you need from Alchemists and Enchanters, or you can take Alchemy, Enchanting, Leatherworking, or Tailoring yourself, supply your own upgrades, and use the extra damage to kill faster and make gold that way.

flow.v: Restoration Druid will continue to be a strong healing class in PvE content. From what has been released, we see incredible efficiency, strong single-target throughput, high raid-wide HoT healing capacity, and the classic defensive recovery of|s20484|and|s29166|to help push our teams over the finish line.

Where Restoration Druids sit in rankings for meta raid compositions will depend on how the other classes are balanced and raid fights are designed. HoT healing is the first to struggle in low raid damage encounters and needs overwhelming damage that lets HoTs tick without being sniped by other classes' direct heals.

The other big question for Restoration Druid is what unique utility we will bring in relation to other healing classes. The utility Restoration Druids have classically provided is "defensive recovery" utility, strong capabilities to pull attempts back from mistakes and outlast unexpected situations. Competitive raids typically look for more offensive utility kits and trust their ability as players to not reach these botched situations in the first place.
Restoration Druids are great healers in the right hands, but some groups may be looking for more than great healing.

flow.v: Restoration Druid is not the most straightforward healing spec for new players. The spec shines in providing efficient healing through HoTs, which need to be applied proactively to handle healing situations. This requires having an understanding of what damage each raid fight could do, and an intuition of who to buff with a HoT when there is no damage to heal.

New players would be more comfortable in a reactive healing playstyle, where you see damage being taken and push a button to heal it up. Restoration Druids do have these buttons to push as well, but what makes Restoration Druids special is the HoT healing that can keep the majority of a raid alive simultaneously with smart play.
That said, Restoration Druid is one of the most versatile healers and one of the most fun healing playstyles. The class is worth the learning curve of figuring out how to heal with HoTs effectively.
